explanations.explanation: "Abner was furious over Ish-bosheth’s accusation." That's the text, friend, no guessing needed (2 Samuel 3:8). Ish-bosheth, Saul's son and the king Abner set up (2 Samuel 2:8-9), questioned the wrong man. I think he expected a quiet "yes, sire" and got a volcano instead.
No chuckling here, friend. The text says Abner "…was furious over Ish-bosheth’s accusation." (2 Samuel 3:8). Nobody opens a speech about dogs and loyalty while giggling.

Abner doesn't beg for anything. The text says he "was furious," and then he fires back with questions of his own (2 Samuel 3:8). He says he has been loyal to the house of Saul and then turns the accusation around on Ish-bosheth. Not a single "please forgive me" in the whole speech.

Close, friend, but Abner says the opposite. His words are, "I have not delivered you into the hand of David…" (2 Samuel 3:8). He is saying he has been loyal to the house of Saul all this time. The speech sounds like a man defending his record, so a handover to David is the one thing he says he hasn't done.

Right, he says the opposite. Abner tells Ish-bosheth, "I have not delivered you into the hand of David…" (2 Samuel 3:8). He says he has been loyal to Saul's house, to his brothers and to his friends. Then he asks why he's accused of wrongdoing over this woman anyway.

Abner says he'll "…establish the throne of David over Israel and Judah, from Dan to Beersheba." (2 Samuel 3:10). That's a big promise from the man who set up Saul's son as king (2 Samuel 2:8-9). He also says it's what "…the LORD has sworn…" to David (2 Samuel 3:9). I think he knew exactly what he was saying.

No temple in this oath, friend. Abner swears to "…establish the throne of David over Israel and Judah, from Dan to Beersheba." (2 Samuel 3:10). He's talking about who rules the kingdom, not a building. The kingdom is what gets transferred, and David's throne is what gets established.

Army is a fair guess, since Abner is the army man (2 Samuel 2:8). But his oath is about the kingdom: to "…transfer the kingdom from the house of Saul and to establish the throne of David…" (2 Samuel 3:10). An army man talking about a throne instead of troops. He's thinking bigger than a battle.

The text says, "…for fear of Abner, Ish-bosheth did not dare to say another word to him." (2 Samuel 3:11). One speech and the king goes silent. You know that moment when someone is so angry that you just stop talking? I think that was Ish-bosheth.

It's the other way around, friend. The text says, "…for fear of Abner, Ish-bosheth did not dare to say another word to him." (2 Samuel 3:11). The king had no comeback. Abner talked, and Ish-bosheth didn't answer back.

Abner says, "Make your covenant with me, and surely my hand will be with you to bring all Israel over to you." (2 Samuel 3:12). A covenant is a solemn agreement between two sides. He's offering his help and asking for David's agreement in return.

Not a sacrifice, friend. Abner asks, "Make your covenant with me…" (2 Samuel 3:12). He wants a solemn agreement between the two of them. In return, he says his hand will be with David to bring all Israel over.

No silver changes hands in Abner's ask. He says, "Make your covenant with me, and surely my hand will be with you to bring all Israel over to you." (2 Samuel 3:12). He's asking for an agreement, not a check. Saves everybody a trip to the bank.

David says, "Do not appear before me unless you bring Saul’s daughter Michal when you come to see me." (2 Samuel 3:13). Michal is David's wife, and he later says so plainly to Ish-bosheth (2 Samuel 3:14). No Michal, no meeting. That's a short guest list.

Merab is another daughter of Saul (1 Samuel 14:49), so you're in the right family, friend. But David names "…Saul’s daughter Michal…" (2 Samuel 3:13). He calls her "…my wife, Michal…" when he sends word to Ish-bosheth (2 Samuel 3:14). Merab doesn't come up in this passage at all.

Rizpah came up earlier, in Ish-bosheth's accusation against Abner (2 Samuel 3:7). But David's requirement is different: "Do not appear before me unless you bring Saul’s daughter Michal…" (2 Samuel 3:13). He says Michal is his wife (2 Samuel 3:14). Rizpah isn't part of his demand.
Ish-bosheth doesn't refuse. The text says, "…Ish-bosheth sent and took Michal from her husband Paltiel son of Laish." (2 Samuel 3:15). David asked, and Ish-bosheth sent and took her.

Right, he doesn't refuse. The text says, "…Ish-bosheth sent and took Michal from her husband Paltiel son of Laish." (2 Samuel 3:15). David asked, and Ish-bosheth acted. Paltiel is the husband she was taken from.
Not David, friend. Abner is the one who speaks. He says to Paltiel, “Go back.” (2 Samuel 3:16). Then Paltiel returns home. Before that, he had followed her, weeping all the way to Bahurim.

Right, it's not David. Abner is the one who speaks: "Go back." Then Paltiel "returned home" (2 Samuel 3:16). Paltiel had followed her weeping all the way to Bahurim before that. I think that one hurts, so it's okay to feel it.

explanations.answer: Save Israel from the Philistines and all their enemies
explanations.explanation: Abner quotes the LORD: "Through My servant David I will save My people Israel from the hands of the Philistines and of all their enemies." (2 Samuel 3:18). He uses it to tell the elders to act now. Notice the words "…My servant David…" That's how the LORD names him.

explanations.answer: Build a house for His name in Jerusalem
explanations.explanation: A house for His name does come up elsewhere (2 Samuel 7:13), but it isn't what Abner quotes here. The LORD says, "Through My servant David I will save My people Israel from the hands of the Philistines and of all their enemies." (2 Samuel 3:18). The elders hear a word about rescue. Nothing about a house is in this speech.

explanations.answer: Lead Israel across the Jordan into a new land
explanations.explanation: Crossing the Jordan belongs to a different chapter of Israel's story, friend (Joshua 3:17). Here Abner quotes the LORD: "Through My servant David I will save My people Israel from the hands of the Philistines and of all their enemies." (2 Samuel 3:18). It's about being saved from enemies. No new land is mentioned.

The text says, "Abner also spoke to the Benjamites." (2 Samuel 3:19). Benjamin was Saul's own tribe (1 Samuel 9:1-2). Then Abner went to Hebron to tell David what seemed good to Israel and the whole house of Benjamin. He was working the room, friend, one tribe at a time.

The Levites aren't who the text names. It says, "Abner also spoke to the Benjamites." (2 Samuel 3:19). Benjamin was Saul's tribe (1 Samuel 9:1-2). Talking to them mattered, since they were Saul's own people.

Ephraim is a fair guess, friend, but it isn't named here. The text says, "Abner also spoke to the Benjamites." (2 Samuel 3:19). Saul came from the tribe of Benjamin (1 Samuel 9:1-2). So Abner went to talk to Saul's own tribe.

The text says, "…David held a feast for them." (2 Samuel 3:20). Abner showed up from the other side of the war with twenty men, and David set the table. That's a warm welcome. I'd have been checking for the exits, friend.
It's the other way around. The text says, "…David held a feast for them." (2 Samuel 3:20). Twenty men from the other side of the war got a table instead of a fight. That's some welcome.

The text says, "So David dismissed Abner, and he went in peace." (2 Samuel 3:21). Abner had just promised to gather all Israel to David. David had held a feast for him and his men (2 Samuel 3:20), and then he left in peace. That's a good way to end a visit.

No chains, friend. The text says, "…David dismissed Abner, and he went in peace." (2 Samuel 3:21). He came with an offer and left with a feast in his belly and a covenant in view. Nobody locked a thing.

Secret is a clever guess, but the text says, "…David dismissed Abner, and he went in peace." (2 Samuel 3:21). Abner told David plainly what he would do: gather all Israel to him. He didn't sneak out. He walked out in peace.
